notes:
I couldn't find notes for every verse, and some of the sources you asked for aren't covered at all. Enduring Word's own site, Wesley, Seedbed, the Lutheran and Pentecostal sites, Bible Odyssey's article on this chapter, and the Catholic and Orthodox sites all failed to load or weren't reached before my tool limit ran out. I did read David Guzik's Enduring Word study on Leviticus 11 through Blue Letter Bible, so it appears below with that URL.

**Overview (vv. 1–24 as a whole)**
- **Why God gave these laws: obedience.** Guzik says the food laws let Israel show obedience and set the nation apart. He compares them to God's first command in Eden, which was also about food. The dietary laws gave the Israelites an opportunity to demonstrate obedience to God... just as the first law God gave to humanity had to do with what could and could not be eaten — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-11.cfm
- **Four common explanations.** Bible.org lists several. One is about pagan worship: certain kinds of creatures were used in pagan ritual and worship. Another is about health, which the writer says is the one Christians love so much today — https://bible.org/seriespage/8-clean-and-unclean-part-i-leviticus-11. Constable adds a third: some animals were "abnormal" for their kind. He also notes that the chapter follows that of the creation of animal life in Genesis 1 (Rashi) — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html
- **What the laws pictured (Wenham, cited by Precept Austin).** The laws kept reminding Israel that God has distinguished them from all the other nations on earth to be his own possession — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_11_commentary
- **Matthew Henry.** He notes that many unclean animals were had in high veneration among the heathen — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html

**v. 1**
- Moses and Aaron receive the food rules together. BibleHub's notes on v. 2 say everything that follows spells out which animals belong in the "may eat" group — https://biblehub.com/q/Leviticus_11_2_Clean_vs_unclean_animals.htm

**v. 2**
- In Mosaic law, "clean" means fit for food and sacrifice. GotQuestions notes that unclean animals could not be used as sacrifices and could not be eaten — https://www.gotquestions.org/rabbits-chew-cud.html
- BibleHub's chapter study notes that in the ancient world diet often indicated allegiance to a deity, so Israel's meals became reminders of whom they belonged to — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11.htm

**v. 3**
- **The NET Bible's note.** The Hebrew reads literally "bringer up of the cud." The note says the verses that follow make clear that both marks were required; one alone was not enough — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Lev&chapter=11
- **Symbolic reading (Catholic, Douay-Rheims notes).** A split hoof and chewing the cud stand for telling good from evil and meditating on God's law — https://www.ccel.org/c/challoner/douayrheims/Leviticus/11.html
- **Symbolic reading (Precept Austin).** Christians should "chew the cud" by meditating on Scripture and show a "separated walk," pictured by the split hoof — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60788/

**v. 4 (camel)**
- **Calvin.** One mark without the other won't do. In his words, Moses taught that partial and imperfect purity must not be obtruded upon God — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html
- **Gill.** He notes that Aristotle also described the camel as chewing like horned cattle — same URL.
- **Pulpit Commentary, quoting Gardiner.** Scientifically, the camel would be said to divide the hoof... But laws for popular use must necessarily employ terms as they are popularly understood — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/11-6.htm

**v. 5 (rock badger)**
- Keil and Delitzsch report that scholars disagree on which animal is meant. Some think the *shaphan* is the jerboa; others, including the Rabbis and Luther, think it is the rabbit or coney — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/11-6.htm
- A sermon collected on BibleHub compares people all for earth to coneys that chew the cud but burrow in the ground — https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/11-2.htm

**v. 6 (rabbit or hare)**
- **The Pulpit Commentary.** Neither the hare, however, nor the hyrax chews the cud in the strict sense of the words. But they have the appearance of doing so. Moses was writing as a lawgiver, not an anatomist — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11-6.htm
- **Ellicott.** Other peoples also avoided hare meat, including the Parsees and the ancient Britons — same URL.
- **Benson.** The hare has a rennet in its stomach like animals that chew the cud, so it is said to chew it — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/11-6.htm
- **Gill.** Moses is the only ancient writer who says the hare chews the cud. Gill also treats the hare as a picture of people given over to lust — same URL.
- **GotQuestions.** The Hebrew phrase is broader than the modern English one. Rabbits re-eat their droppings and chew constantly, so There's no error here. — https://www.gotquestions.org/rabbits-chew-cud.html

**v. 7 (pig)**
- **The health explanation.** Animals that carry more parasites (pigs) or toxins (shellfish) were excluded in a time without refrigeration — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11.htm
- **The pagan-worship explanation.** Bible.org notes that pig bones are found across the ancient Near East in pagan sacrificial settings — https://bible.org/seriespage/8-clean-and-unclean-part-i-leviticus-11
- **The NET Bible's note.** The verb for "chewing" here differs from the one in the earlier verses — https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Lev&chapter=11
- **Matthew Henry.** He draws a moral lesson: We must not be filthy nor wallow in the mire as swine — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html

**v. 8**
- **Bible.org.** It is in its death that the animal contaminates. Even a clean animal killed by a wolf would make the person who ate it unclean — https://bible.org/seriespage/8-clean-and-unclean-part-i-leviticus-11
- **BibleHub's notes on Deuteronomy 14:8.** Contact with a dead pig made a person ceremonially unclean. They add that through Christ, believers are no longer bound by Israel's food laws — https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/14-8.htm

**vv. 9–12 (water creatures)**
- **Guzik.** Most fish were clean. Catfish, which have no scales, were not, and neither were shellfish (clams, crabs, oysters, lobster) — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-11.cfm
- **Symbolic reading (Precept Austin).** Scales stand for the Christian's armour, and fins for the divine power that lets him move through the world without being overcome — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60788/
- **Catholic reading (Douay-Rheims notes).** Unclean fish stand for souls that do not rise up in prayer or cover themselves with "the scales of virtue" — https://www.ccel.org/c/challoner/douayrheims/Leviticus/11.html
- **Pulpit homiletics.** Scaleless creatures belong to mud and marsh, while the clean ones swim in clear water — https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/11-2.htm
- **v. 11, "abomination."** The Hebrew *sheqets* means something detestable. BibleHub stresses that the strong word expresses God's verdict, not just personal distaste — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11-11.htm
- **v. 11, why "detestable."** Bible.org says the aim was for Israel not even to want to eat these creatures — https://bible.org/seriespage/8-clean-and-unclean-part-i-leviticus-11

**vv. 13–19 (birds)**
- **Guzik on what the birds share.** The common thread through most of these birds is that they are either predators or scavengers. He cites scholars who think the reason is that such birds took in their prey's blood — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-11.cfm
- **Constable, drawing on Mary Douglas.** Birds of prey are unclean because they eat carrion and undrained flesh, the same acts that made people unclean — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html
- **Clean birds by omission.** Birds not on the list, such as doves and pigeons used in sacrifice, were clean — https://biblehub.com/q/Leviticus_11_2_Clean_vs_unclean_animals.htm
- **v. 15, "any kind of raven."** BibleHub says the whole raven family is ruled out because ravens eat carrion — https://biblehub.com/q/Leviticus_11_15_Clean_vs_unclean_animals.htm
- **v. 19, hoopoe and bat.** BibleHub links the hoopoe to nesting in decaying matter. It notes the bat is a flying mammal that ends the list — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11-19.htm
- **v. 19, translation.** The bird names vary between Bible versions. For example, Douay-Rheims has "charadrion" and some older versions have "lapwing" — same URL.

**vv. 20–23 (flying insects)**
- **"All fours" (BibleHub).** This is everyday, observational language. To an ancient observer, insects seemed to walk on four main legs — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11-21.htm
- **Adam Clarke.** "All fours" may simply mean walking step by step like four-footed animals, since insects generally have six feet — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/leviticus/11-20.html
- **Clarke on "fowls that creep."** He also suggests the bat is included here, crawling on the claws of its wings — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/leviticus/11-20.html
- **Guzik, quoting Peter-Contesse.** The phrase was probably not literal. It meant "to crawl" and applied to any flyer with more than two legs — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-11.cfm
- **vv. 21–22, locusts.** The big hind legs mark out locust-type insects. John the Baptist later ate locusts — https://biblehub.com/leviticus/11-21.htm
- **vv. 21–22, a typological note.** A Pulpit-era homily remarks that the only clean insects were locusts, which God so often used to judge guilty lands — https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/11-2.htm

**v. 24**
- **The health reading (Guzik).** This uncleanness also protected health. Rules like breaking a bowl a rodent fell into kept disease from spreading and encouraged a clean home — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-11.cfm
- **The Bridgeway Bible Commentary.** It reads "unclean till evening" as a quarantine against germs — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html
- **The ceremonial reading (BibleHub).** The uncleanness was ceremonial, not moral. "Until evening" set a fixed limit, which pointed to God's provision for restoring the person — https://biblehub.com/q/Leviticus_11_27_Clean_vs_unclean_animals.htm

**Where traditions differ**
In what I read, Protestant teachers don't split over what these verses mean. They differ in emphasis, mainly health versus symbolism, and over whether the laws still apply.
- **Calvin and Westminster (Reformed).** BibleHub reports that Calvin called the food laws "abolished, not merely abrogated," and that the Westminster Confession calls them "expired" — https://biblehub.com/q/Leviticus_11_40_s_role_in_modern_diets.htm
- **Mainstream churches versus Adventists.** The same page says mainstream Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox teaching lets believers eat all foods with thanksgiving. Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic congregations keep Leviticus 11 by choice — same URL.
- **Gill and Clarke.** I found verse comments from Gill (Baptist) and Clarke and Benson (Methodist), but on these verses they make factual and symbolic points rather than points that set traditions apart.

**Other views**
- **Modern scholarship (Mary Douglas).** Precept Austin and Constable cite her idea that only "normal," complete members of each kind count as clean. On this view, wholeness pictures the moral wholeness God wants in his people — https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_11_commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/11-4.html
- **Catholic (Challoner's Douay-Rheims notes).** He gives four reasons for the laws: to train obedience and self-control, to restrain the vices these animals symbolise, because most forbidden foods were unwholesome, and to lead people toward spiritual cleanness — https://www.ccel.org/c/challoner/douayrheims/Leviticus/11.html
- **A debated "divine health" view (Everett's Study Notes).** This commentary says the laws were given so Israel could walk in divine health. It also claims they still govern what Christians should eat, based on 1 Timothy 4:4–5 — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/leviticus-11.html. Most of the other sources disagree. GotQuestions, for example, says Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) — https://www.gotquestions.org/Bible-foods.html
